Glass-pane globe stack. Makes the poster and the video of a relief globe with six glass panes, each a different field of one weather forecast, and the inputs of its Remotion version.

This is the executed notebook (outputs kept). The same recipe as a script: 01_glass_stack.py; for Google Colab: 01_glass_stack_colab.ipynb (the badge opens it).

Gallery · this recipe as a web page · repository · Map created by Shammunul Islam

Glass-pane globe stack¶

The picture. A relief globe with six glass panes standing in front of it. Every pane shows the same round patch of the Earth (the cap of 21° around 21°N 87°E: India, Bangladesh, the Bay of Bengal) at the same moment of one weather forecast, each with a different quantity: temperature, sea-level pressure, wind, precipitable water, cloud cover and rain rate. The panes are pulled apart along the line of sight to that patch, so each can be seen, and they line up with the globe behind them.

How to read it. Left: the globe with the region turned towards you. In front of it, fanned to the right: the panes, numbered 1 (nearest the globe) to 6. Right: what each numbered pane shows, with its colour bar. Bottom: the lead time, the valid time in UTC and in Indian Standard Time, the place of that time on the five-day timeline, and the sources. The panes are not at physical heights: they are six maps of one patch, pulled apart.

The data. NOAA GFS forecast, 0.25°, run of 16 November 2026 18 UTC, read from dynamical.org (CC BY 4.0). Relief: ETOPO 2022 (NOAA NCEI). Coastlines: Natural Earth.

Steps: 1 data → 2 the round view of one field → 3 six pane pictures → 4 the globe's skin → 5 globe and panes in 3-D → 6 the finished poster → 7 the animation → 8 the inputs of the Remotion version.

CHANGE IF YOU LIKE — RUN
Settings

Everything you may want to change is in this one cell. The checks at the bottom stop the notebook with a plain message if a setting cannot work, before anything slow starts.

MODE = "FAST" (the default, about two minutes; right for Google Colab) writes the poster at 1920 × 1080 px and a short preview clip of the animation at 960 × 540 px. MODE = "FULL" writes the poster at 3840 × 2160 px and the whole animation (16 s, 1280 × 720 px, 24 frames a second; several minutes).

SOURCE = "shipped" (the default) reads the small data file that comes with the repository: no network to dynamical.org is needed. SOURCE = "live" reads the run RUN straight from dynamical.org, anonymously (first pip install icechunk zarr; about 35 MB, about a minute); if that read fails for any reason, the shipped file is used and a line says so.

In [1]:
import os
import sys

MODE = "FULL" if "--full" in sys.argv else os.environ.get("GIS_MODE", "FAST")   # "FAST" (preview) or "FULL" (poster size, whole animation)
OUT_DIR = os.environ.get("GIS_OUT", "")          # output folder; "" = /content/out on Google Colab, ./out anywhere else
SOURCE = os.environ.get("GIS_SOURCE", "shipped")  # "shipped" (the file of the repository) or "live" (dynamical.org)
RUN = "2026-11-16T18:00"                         # with SOURCE = "live": the GFS run, hour 00, 06, 12 or 18 UTC; None = the newest complete run
LEAD = 66                                        # the lead time of the poster in hours: a multiple of 6 from 6 to 102
CAP = dict(lat0=21.0, lon0=87.0, rad_deg=21.0)   # the cap every pane shows: centre and angular radius in degrees

import datetime as dt

from gismaps import nb                           # helpers: show(), video(), STOP checks, PASS / FAIL

nb.stop_unless(MODE in ("FAST", "FULL"), f"MODE = {MODE!r} must be FAST or FULL")
nb.stop_unless(SOURCE in ("shipped", "live"), f"SOURCE = {SOURCE!r} must be shipped or live")
nb.stop_unless(LEAD in range(6, 103, 6), f"LEAD = {LEAD} must be a multiple of 6 from 6 to 102 (cloud and rain are averages: there is no value at 0)")
if SOURCE == "live" and RUN is not None:
    try:
        _run = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(RUN)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        _run = None
    nb.stop_unless(_run is not None and _run.hour in (0, 6, 12, 18) and _run.minute == 0,
                   f"RUN = {RUN!r} must look like '2026-11-16T18:00' with hour 00, 06, 12 or 18 (or be None for the newest run)")
WORKER = bool(os.environ.get("GIS_PART"))        # (set only in the frame workers of the parallel FULL render: they skip the extras)
POSTER_SCALE = 2.0 if MODE == "FULL" and not WORKER else 1.0   # the design size is 1920 x 1080; the poster is saved at this multiple
OUT = nb.out_dir(OUT_DIR)
print(f"settings OK | mode: {MODE} | data: {SOURCE} | output folder: {OUT} | poster {int(1920 * POSTER_SCALE)} x {int(1080 * POSTER_SCALE)} px")

settings OK | mode: FAST | data: shipped | output folder: out | poster 1920 x 1080 px
RUN
1 · The data

Six fields of one forecast run on the box 0-44°N, 62-112°E at 0.25°, every 6 hours from +6 h to +102 h: temperature at 2 m, sea-level pressure, wind speed at 10 m, precipitable water (the water vapour of the whole column of air, as the depth of rain it would make), total cloud cover, and the precipitation rate averaged over the 6 hours before each lead time. The shipped file keeps them as 16-bit numbers (2 MB).

In [2]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from gismaps.glass import gfs, ortho, panes, render        # the code of this recipe
from gismaps.glass.stack import GlassStack
from gismaps.styles import common as C

ds = gfs.region(SOURCE, RUN)                     # dims (lead, latitude, longitude)
RUN = ds.attrs["run"]
print("run:", RUN, "UTC |", dict(ds.sizes), "|", ds.attrs["credit"])
for k in ds.data_vars:
    a = ds[k].sel(lead=LEAD)
    print(f"  {k:5s} at +{LEAD} h: {float(a.min()):8.1f} to {float(a.max()):8.1f} {a.attrs['units']}")

run: 2026-11-16T18:00 UTC | {'lead': 17, 'latitude': 177, 'longitude': 201} | Data: dynamical.org / NOAA GFS (CC BY 4.0)
  t2m   at +66 h:    -26.8 to     32.8 degC
  mslp  at +66 h:    995.8 to   1061.8 hPa
  wind  at +66 h:      0.0 to     22.6 m s-1
  pwat  at +66 h:      0.2 to     77.5 kg m-2
  tcc   at +66 h:      0.0 to    100.0 percent
  rain  at +66 h:      0.0 to     31.5 mm h-1

2 · The round view of one field

Stand far away, straight above the centre of the cap: what you see is a disc, the orthographic projection. Each pane shows exactly that view, which is why the panes line up with the globe behind them. To make the picture we go backwards: for every pixel of the disc, ortho.inverse gives the place it shows, and ortho.sample reads the field there (bilinear). Going backwards leaves no holes. East is to the right and north is up, as seen from outside the globe.

In [3]:
F = panes.fields(ds, LEAD)                       # the six maps of the poster's lead time (+ a smoothed pressure for the isobars)
lat_px, lon_px, inside, _ = ortho.disc(360, **CAP)          # the place each pixel of a 360 x 360 pane shows
pw = F["pwat"]
disc = np.where(inside, ortho.sample(pw.values, pw.latitude.values, pw.longitude.values, lat_px, lon_px), np.nan)

th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)              # the edge of the cap, drawn on the flat grid
edge_lat, edge_lon = ortho.inverse(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), CAP["lat0"], CAP["lon0"], np.sin(np.radians(CAP["rad_deg"])))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6))
axs[0].pcolormesh(pw.longitude, pw.latitude, pw, cmap=panes.ramp("pwat"), vmin=0, vmax=60, shading="nearest")
axs[0].plot(edge_lon, edge_lat, color=panes.K["amber"], lw=1.8)
axs[0].set_title("the grid as stored: latitude × longitude"); axs[0].set_xlabel("longitude (°E)"); axs[0].set_ylabel("latitude (°N)")
im = axs[1].imshow(disc, cmap=panes.ramp("pwat"), vmin=0, vmax=60, extent=(-1, 1, -1, 1))
axs[1].set_title("the same numbers on the disc (orthographic)"); axs[1].set_xlabel("u (east →)"); axs[1].set_ylabel("v (north ↑)")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axs, shrink=0.85, pad=0.02, label="precipitable water (kg m⁻²)")
plt.show()
RUN
3 · Six pane pictures

A pane picture has four numbers per pixel: red, green, blue and opacity. panes.pane colours the disc with one ramp per quantity and chooses the opacity; then it draws lines on top (isobars every 4 hPa, the coastline), each projected with ortho.forward. The rules, nearest the globe first:

  1. temperature: a two-sided ramp with white at 0 °C;
  2. pressure: a quiet blue-grey fill, the isobars carry the information (drawn from a lightly smoothed copy, because stored pressure comes in steps of 0.64 hPa);
  3. wind speed and 4. precipitable water: one hue each, dark to bright;
  4. cloud: the opacity grows with the cloud cover, so clear sky is clear glass;
  5. rain rate: a logarithmic scale, fully clear below 0.2 mm per hour.
In [4]:
coast = panes.coast_lines("50m")                 # Natural Earth coastline (a small download the first time)
six = panes.six_panes(F, CAP, coast, n=480)      # six dictionaries: the picture "tex" (480 x 480 x 4) and what the legend needs
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(11, 7.4))
for a, P in zip(axs.ravel(), six):
    a.set_facecolor(panes.K["bg"]); a.imshow(P["tex"], extent=(-1, 1, -1, 1))
    a.set_title(f"{P['title']} ({P['unit']})"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
RUN
4 · The globe's skin

The globe needs one picture that wraps around it: a map in plain latitude × longitude (row 0 = 90°N, column 0 = 180°W). panes.relief_texture builds it from ETOPO 2022 heights: light clay for land, slate blue for sea, shaded as if lit from the north-west so that mountains show (the shading is exaggerated), with the coastline drawn in.

In [5]:
elev = gfs.relief()                              # heights in metres on a 10 arc-minute grid
skin = panes.relief_texture(elev, coast)         # 1440 x 2880 x 3, values 0..1
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5)); plt.imshow(skin, extent=(-180, 180, -90, 90)); plt.xlabel("longitude (°E)"); plt.ylabel("latitude (°N)")
plt.show()
RUN
5 · Globe and panes in 3-D

render.render_stack is a small ray caster. For every pixel it follows a straight line from the eye and asks what the line hits: the globe (a quadratic equation) and each pane (one division: where the line meets the pane's plane). The globe is painted first, then the panes from the nearest to the globe outwards, each laid over the picture with its opacity. Rendering at twice the size and shrinking (ss=2) smooths every edge.

The camera sits 42° west of the stack axis and 15° above it, so the panes fan out to the right of the globe. The panes are spaced 0.9 × the disc radius apart, enough for a strip of every pane to be seen.

In [6]:
stack = GlassStack(ds, CAP, place="India and Bangladesh", local=(5.5, "IST"), coast=coast, elev=elev, skin=skin)
cam = stack.fan_camera((1920, 1080))             # the fanned view (az = -42, el = 15)
bare = stack.render(six, cam, ss=1)              # globe and six panes, no labels yet
plt.figure(figsize=(11, 6.2)); plt.imshow(bare); plt.axis("off"); plt.show()
RUN
6 · The finished poster

stack.poster renders the same view with smooth edges and adds what a picture of data needs: a top strap with the title, a legend column with one numbered row per pane (the same number sits on a chip at the pane's upper right corner, found with render.project), the lead time with the valid time in UTC and local time, a timeline, and the credits.

What to look for: the closed isobars on pane 2 over the south-west Bay of Bengal are a low (a region of low pressure that air spirals into). On the panes in front of it you find its bright wind, its plume of precipitable water, its cloud shield and its rain: one system, six views.

In [7]:
poster = stack.poster(OUT / "glass_stack.png", lead=LEAD, scale=POSTER_SCALE)
nb.show(poster)
RUN — A SHORT PREVIEW IN FAST MODE, THE WHOLE ANIMATION IN FULL MODE
7 · The animation

The film is one function of time, stack.film_state(t): it returns the camera, the gap between the panes, each pane's opacity and lift, and the lead time shown, each as an eased blend between keyframe values. In 16 seconds: the globe glides towards the region (0-3 s), the panes fan out (3-5 s), the precipitable-water pane is lifted with an amber edge while the others dim (6-9 s), the forecast clock runs from +6 h to +102 h (9-14 s; the pane pictures are made every 6 hours and cross-faded in between), and the panes close up on the globe (14-16 s).

In [8]:
if MODE == "FULL":                               # the whole animation: 384 frames, 1280 x 720 px
    movie = stack.animate(OUT / "glass_stack.mp4", OUT / "frames_glass")
else:                                            # a short preview: every 4th frame, 960 x 540 px, 8 frames a second
    movie = C.preview(stack.animate, OUT / "glass_stack_preview.mp4", OUT / "frames_glass", thin=4, scale=0.75, fps=8)
nb.video(movie)
RUN
8 · The inputs of the Remotion version

The second film of this recipe (glass_stack_remotion.mp4: five panes over the whole hemisphere centred on 45°N 30°W, drawn with three.js) is rendered by the Remotion project in remotion/glass_stack of the repository. This cell writes everything that project loads: the globe's skin, 40 pane pictures (5 fields × 8 lead times, 900 × 900 px) and a small manifest, from the shipped hemisphere file (0.5°, same run).

The render itself needs Node.js on your own computer; it does not run in this notebook or on Colab. Copy the folder written here to remotion/glass_stack/public, then follow remotion/glass_stack/README.md (npm install, then one npx remotion render command).

In [9]:
from gismaps.glass import remotion

if WORKER:
    manifest = None
else:
    manifest = remotion.write_inputs(OUT / "remotion_public")      # always from the shipped file (a live read is 240 MB)
    print("lead times (h):", manifest["leads_h"], "| North Atlantic low at +36 h:", manifest["atlantic_low"][5])
    nb.strip([OUT / "remotion_public" / f"{f}_5.png" for f in remotion.FIELDS])

wrote relief.png, 40 pane pictures and manifest.json -> out\remotion_public
lead times (h): [6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48] | North Atlantic low at +36 h: {'lead_h': 36, 'hPa': 960.6, 'lat': 52.5, 'lon': -21.5}
RUN — PASS OR FAIL FOR EVERY OUTPUT
Check the outputs

The last cell checks that every output exists and is what it should be, and prints PASS or FAIL per check.

In [10]:
size = (int(1920 * POSTER_SCALE), int(1080 * POSTER_SCALE))
low = float(ds["mslp"].sel(lead=66).sel(latitude=slice(20, 5), longitude=slice(78, 95)).min()) if RUN == gfs.RUN else None
checks = [
    ("the poster exists", poster.exists()),
    (f"the poster is {size[0]} x {size[1]} px", nb.image_size(poster) == size),
    ("six fields at 17 lead times", len(ds.data_vars) == 6 and ds.sizes["lead"] == 17),
    ("six pane pictures, clear outside the disc", len(six) == 6 and all(float(P["tex"][0, 0, 3]) == 0 for P in six)),
    ("the centre of the disc shows the centre of the cap", abs(float(lat_px[180, 180]) - CAP["lat0"]) < 0.2 and abs(float(lon_px[180, 180]) - CAP["lon0"]) < 0.2),
    ("forward and inverse projection agree (Dhaka)", np.allclose(ortho.inverse(*map(np.asarray, ortho.forward(23.81, 90.41, 21.0, 87.0)[:2]), 21.0, 87.0), [23.81, 90.41], atol=1e-9)),
]
if low is not None:
    checks.append(("the low over the Bay of Bengal is there at +66 h (below 1000 hPa)", low < 1000.0))
if not WORKER:                                   # (the frame workers of the parallel FULL render make neither)
    checks.append(("the movie exists and is not empty", movie is not None and movie.exists() and movie.stat().st_size > 20_000))
    checks.append(("the Remotion inputs: manifest, relief and 40 pane pictures", len(list((OUT / "remotion_public").glob("*.png"))) == 41 and (OUT / "remotion_public" / "manifest.json").exists()))
nb.verify(checks)
